stories.headline: Worst in 40 years! Man United script unwanted record after draw against 10-man Spurs
stories.deck: Manchester United recorded their worst league start in nearly 40 years after drawing 1-1 with Tottenham, collecting just six points from six matches. Bryan Mbeumo put United ahead before Dominic Solanke equalised in stoppage time, despite Tottenham playing with 10 men. Spurs manager Roberto De Zerbi praised his team's fighting spirit, while Michael Carrick lamented United’s failure to secure…
stories.bodyText:
Manchester United
 recorded their worst start to a league season in nearly 40 years after being held to a frustrating 1-1 draw by Tottenham Hotspur at Old Trafford on Saturday.
United have collected just six points from their first six 
Premier League
 matches, winning only once and failing to secure victory in their last four games.
Tottenham, meanwhile, remain without a league win after six matches. Despite sitting 18th in the table, manager Roberto De Zerbi was encouraged by his players’ fighting spirit, particularly after they came back to score with 10 men.
Tottenham fight back despite red card
Bryan Mbeumo gave Manchester United the lead against the run of play. Tottenham’s Rodrigo Bentancur was later sent off for head-butting Luke Shaw, giving United a numerical advantage and hope of securing three points.
However, Tottenham refused to give up, with Dominic Solanke heading home a 92nd-minute equaliser to silence the home crowd.
"I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character," De Zerbi told Sky Sports after the match.
Reflecting on his team’s response, he added: "We suffered in the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can."
Despite spending more than £300 million ($397 million) during the summer transfer window, Tottenham have struggled for results. De Zerbi remains confident his approach can work, saying: "We have to believe in ourselves and this football way," and adding, "If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don't play as a team, it is impossible."
United miss another opportunity
Manchester United manager Michael Carrick was disappointed that his team failed to take advantage of Tottenham’s dismissal and secure the win.
"We were mixed (in performance)," Carrick said, admitting his side struggled to find their rhythm in the first half.
United have also failed to win their last three league games against teams that had a player sent off.
"It's a game we should kill off. And we didn't," Carrick said. "Very disappointed to be in a position like that and not come away with the game."

stories.headline: Contemporary Now brings India's evolving art scene to Chennai
stories.deck: Viewing art from a contemporary lens
stories.bodyText: The city of Chennai was transformed into a sweeping canvas for contemporary Indian art in August, as ‘Contemporary Now’ unfolded across galleries, studios, archival centres and cultural institutions. Bringing together nearly 70 artists from different generations, geographies and mediums, the third edition became a meeting point for exhibitions, conversations, walkthroughs and cultural exchanges, offering audiences a glimpse into the country’s evolving art ecosystem. . Built around the curatorial theme ‘Practices in Continuum: Tracing the Present’, the event invited audiences to engage with artistic practices exploring memory, identity, ecology, migration, politics, materiality and the evolving realities of our time. Commencing with the preview of ‘Practices in Continuum: The Work and the World’ at Lalit Kala Akademi, the flagship exhibition brought together presentations from Project 88, Vadehra Art Gallery, Experimenter, TARQ, Chatterjee & Lal, Chemould Prescott Road and Ashvita’s. From there, Contemporary Now expanded across the city over 20 days, with partner exhibitions, artist-led encounters, public discussions, workshops and open houses offering audiences multiple ways to engage with art. .Bengaluru: ‘Read A Kitaab’ litfest opens with conversations on reading, resistance. Discussions ranged from the cultural South and its growing influence on contemporary art to the evolving role of photobooks, publishing and private patronage. . Across the city, audiences could explore exhibitions including ‘Continuiverse: Sculptures by C Krishnaswamy’, ‘In Dialogue with Nature’, George K’s ‘I Have a Dream’, ‘Madras Abstraction’ and ‘Unruly Bodies: Sighting the Body Politic’ from the Avtar Collection, alongside an Open House at Ashvita’s Archival and Conservation Centre. Artist-led walkthroughs, including those by George K and K Benitha Perciyal, offered audiences a closer look at the works and the ideas behind them. . For Priyanjoli Basu, Director of Contemporary Now, the third edition marked a significant evolution from its humble beginnings. “We’ve grown from a single exhibition into a 20-day, multi-venue platform with 68 artists. But the real growth isn’t just in scale but also in depth,” she said. With the exhibition conceived as a continued study of gallery programmes, audiences who had followed Contemporary Now since its first edition could return to artists and galleries across editions and observe how their practices had evolved. “That kind of sustained engagement is what we always hoped for,” she added. . Themes of climate anxiety, migration, political tension and the fragility of memory were not consciously curated into the exhibition; rather, they emerged organically from the works. “When you bring together so many artists from different geographies and generations, certain threads emerge on their own. What connected these artists was not the style but urgency,” Priyanjoli said. . Ashvin E Rajagopalan, Founder of Ashvita’s and Director of Contemporary Now, who worked on the India Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, noted that the practices represented at Contemporary Now were part of a much larger global dialogue. “What Venice did was confirm what we already knew: that Indian artists are having the conversations the rest of the world is also trying to have. India isn’t catching up to the global art scene. It’s offering a perspective the global art scene needs,” he pointed out. While one of the goals was to move beyond Mumbai and Delhi and give Chennai a stronger place in India’s wider art conversation, another was to make contemporary art a way of understanding the world, with different audiences finding their own entry points. . “For a child, it may begin as curiosity. For a student, as a question. For a collector, as a responsibility. What has changed is that the barriers are coming down not because the art has simplified, but because platforms like this one are creating more ways in,” said Priyanjoli.

stories.headline: 4.2-magnitude earthquake hits Uttarkashi, second in Uttarakhand in four days
stories.deck: Officials of the Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) said no damage had been reported so far
stories.bodyText:
A 4.2 magnitude earthquake struck Uttarakhand's Uttarkashi district on Saturday night (October 10, 2026), sending strong tremors across the Uttarkashi town and the Yamunotri valley.
According to the National Centre for Seismology, the earthquake, measuring 4.2, struck at 8.07 p.m., with its epicentre located two km northwest of Uttarkashi at a depth of 11 km.
Purushottam Uniyal, a priest from Kharsali village, the winter seat of Yamunotri, said the tremors were strong enough to cause televisions inside homes to shake. The sudden and intense tremors triggered panic, prompting people to rush outdoors, he said.
Saturday's earthquake was the second tremor measuring above 4.0 on to hit Uttarakhand in four days. A 4.9-magnitude earthquake had struck Chamoli district on October 6.
Officials of the Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) said no damage had been reported so far.

stories.headline: James Patterson's $1.75M gift saved 467 school libraries
stories.deck: James Patterson initially pledged $1.25 million to support US school libraries but increased the donation to $1.75 million. This increase followed an overwhelming response from schools, revealing their pressing needs for resources. A total of 467 libraries benefited from the grants, funding books, technology, and repairs. The American Association of School Librarians recognized Patterson for his…
stories.bodyText:
A flood of requests from schools revealed how badly many libraries needed support, prompting bestselling author James Patterson to increase a donation he had originally planned at $1.25 million. In March 2015, Patterson announced the pledge in partnership with Scholastic Reading Club to help US school libraries buy books and improve their resources. According to the American Association of School Librarians (AASL), the overwhelming response led him to raise the total to $1.75 million, with 467 school libraries eventually receiving grants. The funding could support books, reading programmes, technology and repairs, addressing practical needs that affect how children access reading and learning resources.
A pledge to help school libraries
Patterson announced the initiative on March 9, 2015, working with Scholastic Reading Club to distribute grants to schools across the United States. The programme was designed to make funding accessible to school libraries, with individual grants ranging from $1,000 to $10,000. The author said he was concerned that fewer children were growing up in homes filled with books. He believed access to books and functioning school libraries could influence children's education and encourage a lasting interest in reading.
Scholastic Reading Club helped administer applications through its network of schools and teachers. It also offered recipients additional purchasing support through its Bonus Points programme, which teachers could use to obtain books and classroom materials. The partnership connected Patterson's personal donation with an established education network, allowing the money to reach schools that needed help with their library resources.
Why the donation increased
The response to the announcement was far greater than anticipated. Within two weeks, Patterson and Scholastic had received more than 8,500 applications, according to a March 23, 2015, Scholastic announcement. The volume of requests prompted Patterson to add $250,000 to his original pledge, taking the total to $1.5 million. Demand continued to grow. By June 2015, the partners had received more than 28,000 applications. Patterson then announced another $250,000 increase, bringing the donation to $1.75 million.
The requests highlighted a range of problems facing school libraries. Schools sought money for new books, shelving, classroom materials and repairs, including damage caused by flooding. Others needed resources to improve the spaces in which students read and studied. The response also gave Patterson and Scholastic an opportunity to draw attention to the challenges schools faced in maintaining well-stocked libraries. The programme was intended not only to distribute grants but also to highlight the importance of access to books and reading resources.
How 467 school libraries benefited
The grants were distributed in stages during 2015. In June, Patterson and Scholastic announced the first round of awards, distributing $500,000 among 127 schools. Individual grants ranged from $1,000 to $10,000, while the remaining funds were scheduled for distribution later in the year. The American Association of School Librarians reported in March 2016 that 467 school libraries had received funding through the programme. According to the organisation, the grants supported books, reading programmes, technology and repairs.
These areas of spending addressed different needs. New books could expand the material available to students, while reading programmes could help schools encourage children to develop stronger reading habits. Technology could improve access to educational resources, and repairs could help keep library spaces usable. For schools working with limited resources, even a relatively small grant could address a specific need. The programme allowed libraries to identify their priorities and request funding accordingly, rather than requiring every recipient to spend the money in the same way.
Recognition for a wider literacy effort
Patterson's support for school libraries was part of a broader effort to encourage reading among children. In March 2016, the AASL selected him as the recipient of its Crystal Apple award, recognising his contribution to school library programmes and students. The organisation noted his financial support as well as his advocacy for librarians and reading. Patterson said his aim was to make books available to children in every neighbourhood and encourage them to become lifelong readers.
His partnership with Scholastic also continued beyond the original campaign. In November 2016, the two announced another $1.75 million in school library grants, this time supporting 452 schools. Patterson subsequently extended his education and literacy initiatives to classroom libraries and other programmes. The 2015 pledge demonstrated how a donation can grow when the demand for support becomes clear. What began as a $1.25 million commitment became a $1.75 million programme that helped hundreds of school libraries address their needs, while bringing wider attention to the role libraries play in children's education.

When Spring finds a new movement
briefs.deck: When Spring finds a new movement
briefs.bodyText: It is hard to imagine today, but when Igor Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring premiered in Paris in 1913, shouting matches and disturbances broke out in the audience. Created for the Ballets Russes by Stravinsky and choreographer Vaslav Nijinsky, its radical music and choreography shocked audiences accustomed to classical ballet. More than a century later, it remains a defining masterpiece of 20th-century music and dance. . Reimagining The Rite of Spring through Bharatanatyam was an ambitious undertaking, bringing Stravinsky’s groundbreaking score into dialogue with an entirely different movement tradition. Award-winning British-Asian choreographer and dancer Seeta Patel took on the challenge, creating a striking new interpretation. . Born in London, Patel began training in Bharatanatyam under Kiran Ratna in 1990 and later worked with practitioners, including Mavin Khoo and Adyar K Lakshman. She also performed with contemporary dance companies, including DV8 Physical Theatre and the Shobana Jeyasingh Dance Company. As Artistic Director of Seeta Patel Dance, she brings classical Indian and contemporary dance into dialogue. Her Rite of Spring was nominated for Best New Dance Production at the 2024 Olivier Awards, presented by the Society of London Theatre. .From Homer to Nolan: A seduction for the ages. Seeta Patel Dance recently brought a two-day masterclass on The Rite of Spring to India, with workshops in Bengaluru and other cities for advanced Bharatanatyam dancers. Patel introduced sections of the work, focusing on spatial awareness and on how dancers could engage physically through movement rather than simply performing solo work within a group. . Patel encountered The Rite of Spring only later in life and was drawn to it partly through her interest in ensemble Bharatanatyam, which she had largely experienced as a solo artist and audience member. Though she usually works with Karnatik music, Stravinsky’s rhythmically complex score offered an unexpected affinity with Bharatanatyam. Working with a pianist, she translated the unfamiliar score into patterns, rhythms and syllables for the dancers, while keeping the choreography entirely within the Bharatanatyam vocabulary. Bharatanatyam dancer Adithi Ravi Prakash was struck by this translation: “What fascinated me most was seeing how Bharatanatyam technique responds to a very different musical language.” . Bengaluru-based dancer Tony Pius observed: “Seeta’s choreography uses the same adavus (basic movement units) but rearranges start and end points, giving familiar vocabulary a new lens without abandoning classical grammar. Small movements like a spring in the body are brought to the foreground and built into entire choreographic arcs, rather than used as accents.” The work is rooted in nritta, or pure rhythmic movement, but Patel found that bhava, or emotional expression, could emerge through relationships between dancers and their connection to the music. Rather than conventional group abhinaya, which she feels can become mimetic and literal, she creates emotional qualities through movement, proximity and interaction, allowing feelings such as fear and unpredictability to emerge from the choreography itself. . The music also guided Patel’s thinking about spatial dynamics and the flow of energy between dancers. Inspired by a murmuration of starlings, she wanted the ensemble to constantly shift direction and respond to one another rather than simply form shapes or move “like a marching army.” Adithi found her use of space striking: “Her choreography combines unison with abstraction, moving between small pockets of space and larger expanses.” . Patel’s approach to partnering similarly remained rooted in Bharatanatyam. She avoided lifts and physical contact, instead exploring relationships through rhythm, timing and space. Proximity and negative space create the illusion of one dancer initiating another’s movement. Adithi says Seeta’s approach to structuring space, varying the scale of movement and shifting between intimate and expansive formations will directly inform her own practice as a choreographer, particularly in creating ensemble work. . Patel hopes eventually to bring The Rite of Spring to India with the dancers, scale and artistic integrity the work deserves. The workshops, she says, are an important first step towards bringing the work to Indian audiences.

briefs.headline: Breast cancer: Why awareness and early detection matter
briefs.deck: Why awareness and early detection matter
briefs.bodyText: October is International Breast Cancer Awareness Month. Breast cancer is the commonest cancer affecting women in India. Due to lack of awareness and absence of a robust population-based screening programme, for every two women diagnosed with breast cancer, one dies from the disease. Every eight minutes, a woman in India succumbs to breast cancer. . Unlike the West, where breast cancer is more common after the age of 60, in India the highest incidence is between 40 and 50 years, at least a decade earlier. More than 75 per cent of our population is under the age of 50, making awareness among younger women particularly important. . Unique challenges . Breast cancer in younger women presents unique challenges. The possibility of cancer may never have crossed their minds, and new breast changes may therefore be ignored, resulting in delayed diagnosis. Younger breast tissue is denser, making subtle abnormalities more difficult to detect on mammography. Breast cancer in younger women can also be more aggressive, may respond less well to some treatments and can be associated with poorer outcomes. .Indian scientists develop light-driven nanobots for breast cancer therapy. A new lump or change in the breast should never be ignored, although it is important to remember that not every breast lump is cancer. Most breast lumps are benign. . What matters is seeking appropriate medical assessment rather than assuming either that it is cancer or that it is harmless. Awareness of the normal appearance and feel of one’s breasts can help women recognise a new change. Persistent lumps, changes in breast shape or skin, nipple retraction or blood-stained nipple discharge warrant timely medical evaluation. Early diagnosis ensures simpler treatment, better cosmetic outcomes and, most importantly, saves lives. . Diagnosis at a young age . A diagnosis at a young age can be a profoundly distressing experience. Cancer affects far more than the physical body; it affects mind, body and soul. The concerns of younger women are often very different from those of older women. Counselling is therefore a fundamental component of cancer care. It helps patients and their families understand what lies ahead, prepare for treatment and, importantly, regain a sense of control. Emotional wellbeing and a positive outlook can make an important difference to how patients cope with treatment and life beyond cancer. . Some women are diagnosed during pregnancy or shortly after giving birth — times that should be among the happiest periods of life. Although there is no conclusive evidence that breast cancer during pregnancy is inherently more aggressive, diagnosis can sometimes be delayed because changes in the breast during pregnancy make cancer more difficult to detect. . Treatment depends on the stage of the cancer and the stage of pregnancy, and close coordination between the breast cancer team and the obstetrician is essential. Fertility is another important issue. Some breast cancer treatments can impair fertility, yet women may not raise the subject because they are overwhelmed by the diagnosis, unaware of the potential impact, or uncertain about future plans for children. Doctors should proactively discuss fertility preservation with the patient and her spouse and, arrange referral to a fertility specialist before treatment begins. . Hair loss can be among the most distressing effects of treatment, particularly for younger women. Preparing patients for this possibility, including discussing wigs or hair-preservation approaches such as scalp-cooling systems, can help maintain confidence and a sense of control. Surgery can affect how the breast looks and feels. While mastectomy remains necessary for some women, breast reconstruction can provide an option for restoration. . Advances in surgery . Advances in breast cancer surgery increasingly allow breast-conserving procedures with excellent cosmetic outcomes through oncoplastic techniques. Cancer surgery should always balance oncological safety with cosmetic outcome; unnecessarily disfiguring surgery is neither justified nor acceptable. Oncoplastic surgery combines removal of the cancer with partial reconstruction of the breast defect, with the aims of preserving the breast where appropriate, reducing psychological morbidity and improving patient satisfaction. . Having practised exclusively in breast surgery for many years in both the United Kingdom and India, I have witnessed ordinary women demonstrate extraordinary courage, determination and perseverance. These qualities are often central to navigating the journey through cancer. As Jean de La Bruyère observed, “Out of difficulties grow miracles.” Cancer can be an overwhelming experience, but fear and uncertainty need not define the journey. . Artificial intelligence and health care . The era of artificial intelligence also offers an opportunity to democratise access to trusted breast-health information. National Awareness & Resource Initiative for Breast Health (NARI) is an AI-enabled public health initiative designed to make reliable, evidence-based information on breast health and breast cancer accessible to people across language and geographical barriers. . On this Breast Cancer Awareness Month, I salute breast cancer survivors, or, as I prefer to call them, “breast cancer conquerors” across India. Their courage is a reminder that early recognition, appropriate treatment, compassionate care and hope must go hand in hand. . The author is a surgeon who has received the OBE (Order of theBritish Empire), the Padma Shri and the Dr B C Roy Award.

briefs.headline: Decoding mental illness
briefs.deck: Decoding mental illness
briefs.bodyText: As India approaches the tenth anniversary of the Mental Healthcare Act, mental health has become increasingly visible in public-health conversations. But how much do we actually understand about mental illness? . How our understanding has changed . People have tried to explain unusual behaviour and psychological distress for much of history. Ancient Egyptian medical texts described brain injuries and their symptoms in detail, while physicians in Renaissance Europe and the Islamic world developed medical accounts of the relationship between the brain, body and mental states. At the same time, supernatural and moral explanations persisted, and some continue even today. Psychiatry is much more recent, and approaches mental illness as a complex health phenomenon, as research points to interactions between biology, life experiences and the environments in which people live, rather than a single cause. . More common than we might think . The 2016 National Mental Health Survey of India estimated that about one in ten people live with a mental health condition, while around one in seven have experienced one at some point in their lives. The survey also found a treatment gap of nearly 85 per cent, between those in need of care and those receiving it. These numbers make one thing clear: mental illness is not something that happens only to “other people”. It is an important public health concern affecting every sect of society, making research into its causes, recognition and treatment essential. . No single cause . Researchers study mental illness through many lenses. Brain imaging allows examination of changes in brain structure and function. By studying DNA, they can identify minute changes that may signal vulnerability to a disease. It is even possible now to use donated brain tissue and stem cells carrying a patient's biological footprint to investigate changes linked to diseases that may show up in our cells and molecules. .World Mental Health Day 2026: Expert shares what to expect from a good therapist . Yet, these approaches provide important clues, rather than a complete understanding of the biology of mental illness. Genes, brain development, experiences and environments can all contribute, and their influence differs between individuals. . What does family history mean? . A diagnosis of a mental illness in the family, may cause one to wonder: will I get it too? The answer is not as simple as looking at a family tree. Having a relative with a psychiatric condition can increase vulnerability, but does not mean someone will necessarily develop the same illness. In one study of more than 1,400 people from families with multiple members affected by psychiatric or neurological disorders, researchers found that different psychiatric conditions frequently occurred within the same families — illustrating a complex genetic architecture. Genes may load the dice but do not necessarily determine the numbers rolled. . Life experiences and mental health . Research has linked adverse childhood experiences such as abuse, neglect and household adversity to mental health difficulties, including earlier onset of illness and differences in learning and memory. However, a difficult childhood does not mean mental illness, nor should families be blamed. Substance use provides another example of this complexity. Substance-use disorders often occur alongside mental illnesses, and people experiencing psychological distress may also use substances to cope. Regular or heavy substance use can worsen existing mental-health difficulties or make symptoms harder to recognise and treat, creating diagnostic and treatment challenges for practitioners and patients. If substance use becomes difficult to control, affects relationships, work or daily functioning, or becomes a regular way of coping with distress, it may be worth seeking professional help. . Why India-specific research matters . Much of what we know about mental illnesses comes from Western populations. This has transformed our understanding of illnesses, but raises an important question — are these findings universal? Research across different populations can reveal differences in how illnesses present and progress. Studies in Asian populations, for example, have reported differences in the presentation of bipolar disorder as compared with European populations. Indian studies have also contributed to global evidence that genes associated with the psychiatric risk are active during early brain development. . Indian researchers are contributing to this evidence base. At NIMHANS and National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), the Centre for Brain and Mind’s family-based research brings together clinical, behavioural, neuroimaging and genetic information through CALM-Brain, a repository of mental-health data. . The Centre for Brain Research at IISc has added new perspectives on ageing and neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Other institutions like All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Central Institute of Psychiatry (CIP), Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER) and Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) have a long history of psychiatric and community-based research. . Diagnosis does not define a person's future . Mental illness is not necessarily a lifelong downward trajectory. Timely reporting matters, and a combination of therapy and medication, tailored for each individual, can be majorly effective. Recovery also does not look the same for everyone. It may involve fewer symptoms, but can also mean greater independence, meaningful relationships, education, employment or simply a better quality of life. . This year’s World Mental Health Day theme “lived experiences heard” highlights that people who live with mental illness must be recognised as knowledge holders of what recovery, treatment and support look like in everyday life. This is also why community programmes matter. By bringing mental health conversations into public spaces, they create opportunities to encounter evidence and hear directly from people with lived experience. . Key takeaways . ● A mental illness diagnosis is just a part of a person's life - not their entire identity. ● Family history can increase the risk of developing a mental illness, but it does not mean you will necessarily develop the same/related condition. ● Supportive relationships and safe environments are important particularly for children. ● Persistent distress or major changes in a child's behaviour should not simply be dismissed. ● Alcohol and other addictive substances can worsen or complicate mental health difficulties. If substance use is becoming difficult to control, seek professional help. ● Shifts in mood, behaviour, sleep, functioning, relationships or substance use that persist or interfere with everyday life deserve attention. ● Visiting a psychiatrist or therapist to check on your mental health is just like visiting a doctor to check on your physical health ● Improvement does not look identical for everyone. It can include better symptoms, greater independence, meaningful relationships, education, employment and a better quality of life. . If you need help, call Tele-MANAS, available 24/7 at 14416. . (Y C Janardhan Reddy is Director, NIMHANS and Biju Viswanath is Professor, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS.)

briefs.headline: Breaking bread: A taste of tradition in Georgia
briefs.deck: Breaking bread
briefs.bodyText: The dough felt surprisingly soft in my hands as I tried to stretch it into the elongated shape I had seen Georgian bakers make effortlessly. Under the watchful eye of Ms Eto Iobashvili at Giuaani, a family-run winery in Kakheti, I shaped my first Georgian bread before attempting the trickier part — placing it inside the tone, the traditional clay oven. With a few pointers from Eto, the dough was slapped against the scorching inner wall, where it clung precariously before slowly puffing and browning. Minutes later, I was tearing into warm, freshly baked bread, crisp at the edges and soft and chewy within. . “For Georgian bread, you need high-quality bread flour, fresh yeast, warm milk and a pinch of salt. The quality of these ingredients is crucial, as they directly impact the flavour and texture of the final product,” says Eto. What seemed like a fun bread-making masterclass, however, was an introduction to a culinary tradition with remarkably ancient roots. .A snack worth a little spanking. According to Georgia’s Ministry of Culture, a new international study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences identifies Georgia as one of the world’s oldest independent centres of origin for bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L). The research draws on archaeological evidence from the Neolithic sites of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, dating back nearly 8,000 years. . As I travelled across the country, I began to realise that bread here comes in many shapes, textures and character. . In Tbilisi, I encountered shotis puri again at Republic 24, an upscale café, where the traditional bread sits comfortably alongside a contemporary dining experience. “Foreign travellers love shoti because they find the whole experience authentic, especially seeing bread being baked in a traditional clay oven even at an upscale café,” says Sava Kamarauli, a server at the cafe. . Fresh from the oven, the bread needs little embellishment. Its crust gives way to a chewy centre, making it tempting enough to tear and eat on its own. Yet, another Georgian bread on the same table intrigued mw. It arrived golden, warm and generously filled with cheese: khachapuri. . When cheese meets bread . Calling khachapuri “cheese bread” hardly does justice to it. Almost every region seems to have its own interpretation of the bread, shaped by local ingredients and culinary traditions. The classic Imeruli khachapuri, originating in Imereti, is round and filled with cheese. Megruli khachapuri from Samegrelo has cheese stuffed inside as well as melted over the top. . Perhaps the most recognisable is Adjaruli khachapuri from the Black Sea region of Adjara. Shaped like a boat, it comes filled with molten cheese and topped with an egg yolk and a generous knob of butter. Eating it involves a small ritual: the egg and butter are stirred into the hot cheese before pieces of the crust are torn off by hand and dipped into the creamy centre. . Even the cheeses, grains, and methods used to prepare the bread are not the same across the nation. At Café Salve, I came across lobiani, a bread stuffed with seasoned red beans, and mchadi, the rustic cornbread popular in western Georgia. Then there is nazuki, a subtly sweet, aromatic bread associated particularly with Surami, where roadside stalls tempt passing travellers with freshly baked loaves. A t Vardzia Restaurant, I try meskhetian bread, from southern Georgia, which reflects the region’s old baking traditions, and chvishtari, a hearty cornbread enriched with cheese, giving it a crisp exterior and a warm, gooey centre. . A supra gathering . But perhaps the best place to understand the importance of bread is not a bakery at all. It is at a supra. “A Georgian supra has the warmth of gathering around a table at home,” says local guide Ia Gebrandze. “There is homemade bread, wine and an abundance of dishes to share, but what really matters is being together. Food is our way of welcoming people and making them feel part of the family.”

briefs.headline: Personality rights: HC asks Amitabh Bachchan to appear if settlement fails
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Delhi HC has asked 
Amitabh Bachchan
 to appear in person if a settlement with several defendants in a personality rights case remains incomplete and he still wishes to pursue his claims.
Justice Purushaindra K Kaurav passed the direction after the court was informed an amicable settlement had been reached with some defendants through mediation, but could not be formally signed due to logistical issues on Bachchan’s side.
The court granted time to the actor to complete formalities and place the formal agreement on record. The next hearing will be on Nov 16.
The HC said in the event of a non-settlement or incomplete settlement, Bachchan would have to be personally present if he wished to pursue any of his claims. His presence would enable the court to exercise its powers under provisions of Code of Civil Procedure and Section 168 of BSA, the order underlined. Section 168 empowers a judge to ask any question about any fact s/he considers necessary.

stories.headline: Delhi man caught soliciting money at Bengaluru airport terminal
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 City police have booked a Delhi-based man for allegedly soliciting money from passengers at Kempegowda International Airport (KIA) by claiming he had missed his flight and lacked money to continue his journey.
The 37-year-old man, identified as Ameen of south Delhi, claims to be a businessman. 
Central Industrial Security Force
 (CISF) personnel detained him Friday evening following complaints from passengers that he was harassing people near the arrival gate for money. He was handed over to KIA police later.
Ameen initially repeated his story but confessed when asked to produce the ticket for the flight he claimed to have missed. His travel history showed he had arrived at KIA from Mumbai on Sept 30 night and flown to Chennai on Oct 3 morning.
“CISF personnel received complaints from passengers and, after questioning him briefly, handed him over to us. We booked a non-cognisable case against him for misleading the public before letting him off,” a police source said.
Ameen is said to have sought between Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 from passengers emerging from the arrival gate. His fluent English and confident manner convinced some people to believe his story. “He claimed to have collected around Rs 3,000 from different people before he was caught. However, many passengers he approached refused to help him,” the cop said.

stories.headline: Bengaluru’s traffic is giving commuters a gut feeling — and it’s not a good one
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: The time Bengalureans spend in traffic is taking a toll not only on their mental health but also on their physical health. Gastroenterologists in the city say that long commutes and lifestyle changes trigger digestive problems and aggravate existing gastrointestinal conditions.
From skipping breakfast to get a head start on morning traffic to postponing bowel movements because of unexpected delays on the way home, several commuting-related habits can disrupt digestive health. Prolonged sitting and inadequate water intake can also contribute to problems, doctors said.
According to Dr CM Parameshwara, founder of Smiles Institute of Gastroenterology, 5-10% of his patients report lifestyle patterns linked to long commutes and irregular daily routines. “Traffic doesn’t directly cause gastrointestinal disease. Think about what a two-hour commute can do to your routine. You may postpone going to the toilet because you are stuck on the road, drink less water because you don’t know when you will find a washroom, miss your usual mealtime, and reach home too late to exercise,” he said.
Dr Kiran S, additional director, gastroenterology, Fortis Hospital, Yeshwantpur, said, “Common problems associated with long commutes include constipation, bloating, heartburn, indigestion and irregular bowel movements. 
Inadequate water intake can make stools harder and more difficult to pass, while repeatedly postponing bowel movements may contribute to constipation over time. Prolonged sitting can also reduce overall physical activity, further increasing the risk of constipation in some people.”
Dr Rishabh Agarwal, consultant–medical gastroenterologist, Prakriya Hospitals, said the stress associated with long commutes could also affect the gut-brain axis. “Being stuck in traffic for prolonged periods can cause chronic stress. When you are stressed, hormones such as cortisol increase in the body, and these can adversely affect the gut. This may manifest as bloating or altered bowel habits. This is largely due to what is known as the gut-brain axis, through which the gut responds to stress in the brain,” he explained.
He added that exposure to air pollutants during long commutes could also affect gut health. Some pollutants have been associated with gastrointestinal problems and may be linked to certain cancers.

stories.headline: Residents bat for public transport over elevated corridor in south Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Adding to the continued resistance against Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure Limited’s (B-SMILE) elevated corridors project, residents of Jayanagar and surrounding areas are now opposing the proposed 18.5-km elevated corridor from Ragigudda Junction to Kanakapura Road in south Bengaluru, which will be tolled.
Nearly three residents’ associations have called for a human chain near the proposed alignment on Sunday to raise awareness among citizens about the impact of the elevated corridor.
The opposition follows strong resistance from residents of Indiranagar, C.V. Raman Nagar, and HAL against the elevated corridor between Old Madras Road and Silk Board Junction. Separate groups in east Bengaluru have been opposing the project, with one of them conducting an independent, citizen-led survey of trees to assess the impact on green spaces.
In August, the B-SMILE floated tenders for the Ragigudda corridor, prompting residents to consult traffic and transport experts and review the Detailed Project Report (DPR).
Green spaces and land acquisition
Guruprasad D.N., one of the organisers, said a major concern was the need for the flyover. “There is already metro connectivity along the alignment currently planned by the B-SMILE. The actual requirement is to fix first- and last-mile connectivity,” he said.
The group also pointed out that the alignment passes through Rose Garden and Pipeline Road, both of which have extensive green spaces. Besides, the project also requires forest land near the NICE Road.
According to the official documents, the project requires 16,445 sq. m of government land, including corporation and forest land, as well as 13,481 sq. m of private land. Mr. Guruprasad said the private land requirement covers 24 properties.
The group also flagged that the elevated corridor would pass within a few feet of private properties, causing inconvenience to several households along the alignment.
Growth demands
B.S. Prahallad, Technical Director of B-SMILE, defended the project, citing the year-on-year traffic growth indicated in the DPR.
“We agree that it will be an inconvenience to local residents, be it during the acquisition or construction period, but a substantial number of commuters will gain from the corridor. These corridors are planned with the future in mind,” he said.
Public transport could help
The DPR states that the traffic capacity of most junctions along the proposed corridor has already exceeded their design capacity of 10,000 Passenger Car Units (PCUs) per hour, requiring immediate intervention to prevent bottlenecks.
The corridor primarily covers seven junctions — Rose Garden, Sarakki Junction, Konanakunte Cross 1 and 2, A2B Junction, 80 Feet Road Junction, and Turahalli Junction — where PCU growth is projected to be nearly 90% over 10 years.
For instance, the PCU count at Rose Garden in 2025 was 6,169, which is projected to rise to 11,599 by 2035. However, the DPR also offers two options to meet the growing demand, including policy changes, a modal shift, and the promotion of public transport.

briefs.headline: 461 plot owners in approved layouts hit by PRR-2 notification in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Property owners in layouts near south Bengaluru’s Kaggalipura are shocked that their plots in approved layouts, bought as recently as seven months ago, have been notified for acquisition for Peripheral Ring Road-2 (PRR-2). They alleged that Bangalore Development Authority’s compensation offer is barely 10% of the current land value of Rs 2,000 per sqft.
No fewer than 461 plot owners in two layouts are said to have been affected by the notification, covering more than four acres. The final notification covers 1,427 acres across 31 villages in Bengaluru Urban district.
Now, they have questioned the credibility of govt approvals for land projects and Bangalore Metropolitan Region Development Authority-approved layouts, while seeking denotification of the affected properties.
Owners of residential layouts, The Gardens-4 and SLV Krishna Gardens in Gulakamale off Kanakapura Road, alleged that BDA had failed to account for developments in the area since the project was first notified in 2005-06. The final notification for PRR-2, proposed to run parallel to NICE Road, was issued on Sept 3, 2026.
The owners said they had invested in the sites after checking the layouts’ approval status. According to them, The Gardens-4 received provisional approval from Kanakapura Planning Authority in Dec 2021 and was registered with Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority (Rera) in Oct 2022. 
Sites were subsequently released in phases for registration and khata in 2023.
“With uncertainty over jobs in the IT industry and lack of pension, we had hoped land would be a safety net for us,” said Deepa, a site owner. Divya, another owner, said she had checked the approval status on the BMRDA and Rera websites before purchasing her site. “The registration process was also smooth. However, now the notification lists the properties as part of dry land under the previous owners’ names before the layout was developed,” she said.
According to a senior BDA official in charge of land acquisition, the agency is planning to offer five options for compensation on the lines of PRR 1: cash, transferable development rights (TDR), floor area ratio (FAR), and developed residential and commercial plots. “Proposal for this will be sent to govt for approval. It may take 10-15 days,” the official said.
He declined to comment on BMRDA and Rera approvals for layouts on the alignment. “We can only say BDA had notified these lands before approval was given by those authorities,” he said.
He said many property owners have been approaching BDA seeking compensation as there have been several transactions over the years. “Even if the current owners’ names do not figure in the notification, we have clarified that compensations will be awarded to the site owners,” he added.

briefs.headline: Beyond brochures: Bengaluru schools open doors to woo parents
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Choosing a school is not child’s play. For parents weighing admission options, glossy brochures, campus tours and promises of holistic education may not be enough. They want to see how a school thinks, feels and functions, and whether their children will thrive there.
With the admission season kicking off, several city schools are opening their campuses to the public through events that give prospective families a taste of their educational philosophy, culture and community. From traditional Bengaluru games to skateboarding, fitness, woodworking and discussions on global affairs, these initiatives offer parents and children a preview of school life and help them make informed choices.
School of India, Bannerghetta Road, recently hosted ‘Old Bangalore Vibes’, an event for children aged three to eight and their parents. Activities included hopscotch, Chowka Bhara and clay modelling.
“It was an opportunity for families to reconnect with Bengaluru’s cultural heritage while experiencing the spirit of School of India. Rather than relying on traditional marketing approaches, we wanted to create a space where parents and children could engage with us in a meaningful and enjoyable way,” said Uma Maheshwari, a faculty member.
The event reflected the school’s emphasis on cultural rootedness, experiential learning and community. “The overwhelming response was heartwarming and reinforced our belief that authentic experiences can communicate far more about a school’s philosophy than conventional outreach,” she added.
At School of Raya, on Hennur-Bagalur road, public events aim to bring the school and the wider community together, with attracting prospective parents being just one objective. “A school is a part of its community. At Raya, we believe learning happens when people come together, participate, explore and contribute. Inculcating interest in the school is only one part of it,” said Ambica, outbound and enrichment coordinator.
The Unbusy Project brings women together through fitness and well-being, while Rumble Skate attracts professional and amateur skateboarders. The school’s model G20 initiative allows students to engage with global issues and encounter different perspectives.
Anandi School on Sarjapur Road offers masterclasses, global programmes and private previews for students. Activities range from building electronic products and working in a woodworking lab to hands-on sessions inspired by films. “It is important that children like the school they are moving to. We hope these activities excite students about school and thus make transitions easier,” said Prachi Pawar, the school’s founder.
Stonehill International School also uses public events to showcase the school’s philosophy, giving the community a deeper understanding of how the school thinks. “At Stonehill, we believe learning extends beyond the classroom. Our events and initiatives create opportunities for students and families to put our values into action, while opening our doors to the wider public,” said Joe Lumsden, head of school.
For parents, these events offer more than a look at classrooms and facilities. They can observe how children interact with the campus, which activities spark their curiosity and whether the school’s approach suits their family. For schools, the events provide an opportunity to build relationships with prospective families through shared experiences rather than sales pitches.

briefs.headline: If India plays its cards right, suspension of PERM may be an opportunity: Priyank Kharge
briefs.deck: Karnataka’s IT-BT Minister discusses the potential implications of the suspension, the State’s AI skilling roadmap, its approach to sustainable data centres and plans to build a deep-tech ecosystem focused on solving real-world problems.
briefs.bodyText:
The U.S. government has suspended eight major technology companies, including Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCLTech, from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, a key pathway for employer-sponsored green cards. The move could make future employment prospects uncertain for Indian tech workers and raise costs for Indian companies.
IT-BT Minister Priyank Kharge, however, sees an opportunity to attract investments by strengthening the State’s talent pool.
In an interview with The Hindu, he discusses the potential implications of the suspension, the State’s AI skilling roadmap, its approach to sustainable data centres and plans to build a deep-tech ecosystem focused on solving real-world problems.
What are the implications of the PERM certification changes for Indian tech workers and companies?
It makes the prospects for future applicants uncertain. This could increase costs for Indian companies. Attrition could also become a concern, depending on the sector.
However, if India plays its cards right and sends the right signals, investments will come to the talent rather than talent having to move to where investments are. Bengaluru is a magnet because investments are concentrated here, drawing talent from across Karnataka and India.
But is there enough AI talent to cater to the high-value jobs that may come to India?
Bengaluru is number five globally in AI skillsets as an ecosystem. And we are improving constantly. Whether it is AI across sectors or any other frontier technology, we are up for it.
And as a government, we have been talking to everybody — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Sarvam... We are ready, we have the appetite, and we are bringing in the required policies.
Q: What is Karnataka’s AI roadmap?
We want to have a strong foundation of skills, and that will only come through heavy STEM education and filling the gaps in higher education. Because the courses don’t match the industry standard.
We are talking to the industry, figuring out what they want, and filling in the gap by paying 40% of the costs. So whether it’s coming up with AI labs, AI university or AI incubators, our focus is on building skillsets and trying to create more value-add through IPs. I’m trying to ensure more people re-skilled and employable.
I want to have the most employable human resource in the world. If you do that, investments will follow.
Does Karnataka have specific targets for AI skilling and employment?
We have the appetite. Around 40% of the entire engineering research and development workforce is here. We probably have the most employable graduates in India right now. Around 43% of all tech investments have come to Karnataka in the last nine months. People are coming and investing in Karnataka because we have the right ecosystem of human resources and policies.
The government too is ready to learn, unlearn and relearn. We scrapped our data centre policy, and came up with a sustainable data centre policy. We scrapped our IT policy and came up with a new policy. We came up with the AI University because we have our ear to the ground.
You have spoken about using Bhashini in citizen services. Which government services are being considered for this?
We are agnostic. We are talking to everybody irrespective of which company or which geography you are from. If you are going to help solve a government problem, we are ready to look at you. And that’s why we have done the government-first initiative. No state in India has such a scheme.
We want to ensure that the government not only becomes your first client, but is also your partner in progress, and more importantly, that the positive disruption that these people are bringing in their vertical can be replicated in government departments, too.
But do you think there’s a certain risk in using many of these technologies for citizen service?
It will not be on scale. We will test it out in a regulatory sandbox environment.
Why does Karnataka’s sustainable data centre policy incentivise the use of treated water and green electricity instead of making them mandatory?
Data centres come with a lot of environmental baggage, but it is not unsolvable. That’s why we’ve come up with the sustainable data centre policy, which rewards water and power usage effectiveness. We will do everything possible to ensure that their environment impact is as little as possible.
Wouldn’t making the use of green electricity and treated water mandatory for data centres be more effective?
We are already a green electricity surplus State. We are the second-biggest in solar. I think 65% of all energy is renewable, and we are working to increase that further. By default, it should be green across sectors, not just data centres. The Department of Information Technology is being extremely mindful of being sustainable.
We asked companies to donate computers rather than junk them so we could reuse them in rural schools and government offices. In these places, computing is limited to data entry and basic browsing. We recently redistributed around 4,000 computers State-wide.
Will Karnataka mandate data centres to report their water and electricity consumption to the government?
Eventually, data centres will have to furnish that data as part of the compliance process.
Is there interest from data centre operators in cluster beyond Bengaluru?
Many data centre operators have been talking to us. It’s very easy to say yes to everything, to every hyperscaler. But Karnataka is not interested in a race to the bottom.
What more can we expect for deep tech start-ups from the government?
For the next 10 years, we are concentrating on deep tech only. This time, we are seeking partnerships from the private sector for incubators, accelerators, co-investment with the government, pilots within the government and so on.
People are talking to us, we are experimenting with them, and we are seeing how we will be able to solve real-life problems. The idea of deep tech is to add value.
I’m not interested in the valuation game or unicorn game. I’m interested in seeing whether an innovation solves a problem plaguing the government. Can I deliver better using a particular deep tech innovation?
For example, we are working with some space tech companies. They may be space tech, but their technology will have applications downstream too for disaster management, agriculture, horticulture or oceanography. We have the appetite to absorb all, especially deep tech that can scale and solve real life problems.

briefs.headline: Anti-CEC protest in Bengaluru: Members of Left student groups detained at Freedom Park before march
briefs.deck: The protesters were planning to march to the office of the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer, located a few hundred metres from Freedom Park, but were detained by Bengaluru Police even before they could begin their peaceful protest.
briefs.bodyText:
Over 110 students from the All India Students’ Association (AISA), All India Students’ Federation (AISF), All India Democratic Students’ Association (AIDSO) and Students’ Federation of India (SFI), who were protesting against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, were detained by the Bengaluru city police on Saturday (October 10, 2026).
The students said they were protesting peacefully at Freedom Park, the designated protest site, when the police detained them.
The protesters were planning to march to the office of the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer, located a few hundred metres from Freedom Park, demanding the CEC’s resignation and that all deletions from the electoral rolls, including the 1.07 crore names reported as absent, shifted or dead at the draft stage, be scrapped.
However, the students said that the police detained them before they could begin the march, while they were still within the premises of Freedom Park. The protesters said “barricades had been put up at both ends of the protest site, and they had not crossed the barricades or moved towards the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer’s office when the police suddenly detained them and took them away in buses.”
However, Bengaluru City Police Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh said permission had been granted only for the protest, and not for the march to the CEO’s office. The protesters were, therefore, taken into preventive detention for trying to go attend the march.
Protesters taken away in different buses
Other students from AISA told The Hindu that the police took the protesters away in different buses and that they were trying to contact them to find out where they had been taken. They said they were unable to ascertain whether the detained protesters had been taken to different locations or were all being held at the same police station. “We later found that protestors were taken to Chamrajpet police station.”
“Initially, some protesters were at a police station, while others were trying to establish contact with those detained. We had told the police that we will stage another agitation at the police station itself if the detained students are not released,” AISA members said, adding that the protestors were released by 5 p.m.
Suppression of ‘right to protest’
AISA Karnataka and other Left student organisations condemned the detentions, pointing that the police were suppressing the democratic right to protest. The students association said hundreds of police personnel had been deployed and roads barricaded on both sides to prevent protesters from reaching the Karnataka CEO’s office.
AISA also questioned the Congress-led Karnataka government’s handling of the protest, asking how it differed from the BJP when it came to restricting dissent. It pointed out that the Congress, too, had been opposing the SIR at a national level and demanded that it be scrapped, and questioned why the right to protest was defended at places where a party was in opposition but restricted when it was in power.

stories.headline: SEBI to issue guidelines on CAS in a week: Chairman Pandey
stories.deck: SEBI had sought public comments till October 3 on proposals to review certain aspects of the CAS mechanism, market timings and the settlement methodology for derivative contracts
stories.bodyText:
Markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is expected to issue guidelines on determining derivative settlement prices on expiry days within a week, following a review of the Closing Auction Session (CAS) mechanism, its chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Saturday (October 10, 2026).
SEBI had sought public comments till October 3 on proposals to review certain aspects of the CAS mechanism, market timings and the settlement methodology for derivative contracts.
"Following a review of the Closing Auction Session, a consultation paper was put out to address concerns in respect of the settlement price of derivatives on expiry day. We are currently examining the comments and hope to issue guidelines in about a week's time," Mr. Pandey said at an event organised by the BSE Brokers' Forum.
SEBI had received around 20,000 comments on the consultation paper till 7 p.m. on October 3, 2026, the regulator had said in a post on X.
The CAS mechanism aims to determine closing prices through an auction process.
In September, SEBI proposed changes to the CAS framework and the methodology for determining settlement prices of index and stock derivatives on expiry days. The review followed the introduction of CAS in the equity cash segment and concerns over its impact on derivatives settlement prices.
Separately, Mr. Pandey said SEBI is reviewing the Depositories and Participants Regulations to simplify rules and strengthen fraud prevention. The regulator is also exploring a graded compliance framework for brokers based on their scale, client exposure and technology dependence.
"We are exploring graded compliance based on scale, client exposure and technology dependence. One size need not fit all," he said.
SEBI is also addressing concerns over certain transactions, including tender offers, share buybacks and offers for sale, remaining outside the interoperability framework and requiring parallel clearing arrangements.
He added that implementation of the proposed changes is targeted for the end of November 2026.
The move is expected to improve capital efficiency and reduce compliance costs while maintaining settlement safety.
On easing access to Indian markets for overseas investors, Mr. Pandey said Sebi had consulted on simplifying digital onboarding for Persons Resident Outside India without requiring their physical presence. The regulator has received more than 400 comments on the proposal and will issue a circular shortly.
He also said SEBI is strengthening business continuity, disaster recovery, cybersecurity safeguards and governance across market infrastructure institutions.
“The regulator will soon issue guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, adopting a tiered approach with clear accountability, data controls, kill switches, and human oversight,” Mr. Pandey said.

stories.headline: Landlord wanted tenant out for law office; Delhi HC rejects tenant's objections
stories.deck: Two landlords, who were practising advocates, said they needed the rented premises to set up a law office. The tenant argued that the landlords had changed their stated purpose for seeking possession and already had other properties that could be used for their professional work. The tenant opposed the eviction and applied for leave to defend.
stories.bodyText:
Tenant and landlord disputes are not uncommon and can sometimes turn into legal battles.
In one such case two landlords wanted the tenant to vacate the property so they could open a law office, but the tenant refused and the matter went to court.
The judgment was delivered by 
Delhi High Court
 on September 8, 2026.
What the case is about
Two landlords, who were practising advocates, said they needed the rented premises to set up a law office. The tenant argued that the landlords had changed their stated purpose for seeking possession and already had other properties that could be used for their professional work.
Also Read | 
Woman buys Rs 1.03 crore 3BHK in Bengaluru, but builder fails to provide specially-enabled parking; Karnataka RERA orders provision within 60 days and audited maintenance accounts
The dispute arose from an eviction petition filed by a landlord and another respondent under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The two respondents, both practising advocates, sought possession of the premises to run a law office.
The tenant opposed the eviction and applied for leave to defend. The Additional Rent Controller at Karkardooma Courts rejected his application on April 7, 2026, and passed an eviction order. The tenant then approached the High Court.
His challenge rested on three main arguments. He disputed the landlord-tenant relationship, questioned the genuineness of the stated requirement and claimed that the respondents already had other accommodation that could serve as a law office.
On the first issue, the tenant said he had been a tenant of the respondents’ ancestors and had not formally recognised the respondents as his landlords. He also pointed to the fact that rent had subsequently been paid to another member of the family.
On the question of need, he argued that the respondents had initially sought the premises for a confectionery shop but later changed their stated purpose to a law office. He said that this change cast doubt on whether their requirement was genuine.
The tenant also identified other properties that he believed could be used for the respondents’ professional work.
Also Read | 
US-based daughter files case against parents seeking share in properties; Karnataka HC rejects her ‘ancestral’ claim, saying they were father's separate assets, not coparcenary property
Why did the tenant lose the case?
The court first addressed the landlord-tenant relationship. It noted that the tenant had acknowledged in his own pleadings that the property originally belonged to the respondents’ grandfather, who was the landlord, and that their father later received rent.
The Delhi High Court said that a landlord in proceedings under Section 14(1)(e) need not establish ownership to the same standard required in a title suit.
The relevant question was whether the landlords could demonstrate a better title than the tenant.
The Delhi High Court that changing or refining the intended use does not, by itself, make a requirement mala fide. What mattered was whether the requirement ultimately put forward was genuine.
Both respondents were practising advocates, a fact the tenant himself had admitted in his application. The High Court found no material suggesting that the proposed law office was merely a pretext to secure the tenant’s eviction.
The question of alternative accommodation required closer examination. The rent controller had considered the properties cited by the tenant individually, and the High Court found no basis to disturb those findings.
Also Read | 
Grandmother and her son gifted 2.5-acre land to his second wife, who sold it; his daughter from first marriage claimed it was ancestral, but Madras HC rejects her plea
A chamber in a district court was acknowledged to exist, but the respondents said it belonged to their late father and was too small to accommodate the three advocates concerned, including the wife of one respondent.
Another property was also acknowledged to exist. However, the respondents maintained that it was used as a residence, not an office. The court additionally noted its distance from another district court, where the respondents principally practised.
Then there was the issue of the two shops: The Delhi High Court noted that a family settlement was reached in 2016, under which the shops and property were allotted to other members of the family. The ARC had examined the memorandum recording the family settlement and reached the same conclusion.
Adnan Siddiqui, Partner at King Stubb and Kasiva, told ET that the tenant's own admission that the landlord's grandfather originally owned the property and he was the one to give it on rent to the tenant, made it difficult for the tenant to walk back from it.
Siddiqui explained that courts have repeatedly recognised that, in such proceedings, a landlord needs to establish a title better than that of the tenant.
Another key issue was whether the landlords genuinely needed the premises. Siddiqui noted that tenants sometimes interpret a change or refinement in the reason given for seeking possession as proof that the requirement is not genuine. However, a change in the stated purpose, by itself, does not establish bad faith.
Also Read | 
Man sells ancestral agricultural land for Rs 8 crore, buys two properties and claims LTCG exemption; faces Rs 6.36 crore tax additions, why ITAT Chandigarh gave relief under Sections 54B and 54F
Courts have consistently held that the landlord is best placed to decide how to use their property. It is for the tenant to produce substantive evidence showing that the claimed requirement is merely fanciful or that a genuinely suitable alternative property is already available.
Siddiqui said tenants facing eviction proceedings should pay particular attention to the leave-to-defend stage. This is generally the critical opportunity to raise an issue that warrants a trial, especially given the absence of an appellate remedy. Before filing the application, tenants should carefully consider the legal consequences of every assertion, particularly statements that could be treated as admissions regarding ownership or the suitability of alternative premises.
Finding no jurisdictional error, material irregularity or perversity in the rent controller’s decision, the High Court dismissed the tenant’s revision petition.

stories.headline: ‘To be finalised in line with changed circumstances’: Piyush Goyal on India-US trade deal
stories.deck: India and the US are finalizing their interim trade agreement framework, as circumstances have changed since February. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal indicated that negotiations would consider recent shifts in the US tariff landscape. Trade talks are also progressing with other countries, including Canada and Mexico. Goyal emphasized the need for legal expertise in negotiating comparative…
stories.bodyText:
India and the US will finalise their interim trade agreement framework in line with changing circumstances, commerce and industry minister 
Piyush Goyal
 said on Saturday, indicating that negotiations on the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement (BTA) are continuing.
The two countries announced a framework for an interim trade agreement in February. However, Goyal said the situation had since changed and would have to be considered before the pact is finalised.
“USA (trade pact) February me announce hua. Thodi paristhitiyan badli hain, usko abhi madde nazar rakhte hue final hoga,” Goyal said while addressing members of industry chamber PHDCCI. [It was announced in February. Some circumstances have changed; the final decision will be made keeping that in mind.])
The shifts in the US tariff landscape have led to further negotiations on the first phase of the trade agreement. India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods than those faced by competing countries in the American market.
This comes a day after Goyal said on Friday that trade negotiations with the US were progressing steadily, with both sides working on the fine print. 
Speaking at the ET Startup Awards 2026 in Bengaluru, he said the key issue was securing the comparative advantage for Indian goods that the two countries had agreed upon in February.
“The key issue is how the US will give us the comparative advantage we had agreed upon in Feb. That requires legal expertise, which AI cannot provide, because this goes beyond the textbook. That is what we are working on,” Goyal said.
Meanwhile, earlier this month, Goyal met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers’ meeting in Milwaukee, where the two discussed issues related to the proposed pact.
Goyal also outlined India's wider trade negotiations, saying talks were under way with several countries and regional groupings, including Israel, Chile, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Negotiations with Canada are progressing at a faster pace, while talks on an agreement with the South African Customs Union (SACU) are expected to begin soon. Discussions with Mexico are scheduled to be launched next week, he said.
The minister added that the trade ministers of the UK and Canada would visit India next week. The UK minister's visit will include the India-UK Joint Economic and Trade Committee (JETCO) meeting. India and the UK implemented their trade agreement in July.
His remarks came after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said a deal was not imminent and Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said negotiations had reached a plateau.

briefs.headline: As oil prices increase, RBI opens special window for PSU oil firms to meet their daily dollar needs
briefs.deck: The facility will come in effect from October 12, 2026 and will remain in place until further notice, the central bank added
briefs.bodyText:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday announced a special dollar window to meet the entire daily foreign exchange requirements of three public sector oil marketing companies (OMCs), in a move aimed at easing pressure on the rupee amid rising crude oil prices.
The facility will enable Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOCL), Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (HPCL) and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (BPCL) to procure dollars directly from the central bank through designated banks, reducing their dependence on the spot foreign exchange market.
“On the basis of assessment of current market conditions, Reserve Bank of India has decided to open a special window to meet the entire daily dollar requirements of three public sector oil marketing companies,” the apex bank said in a notification. The facility will take effect on Monday, October 12, and remain operational until further notice, the central bank said.
The three OMCs are estimated to require about $300 million daily to finance crude oil imports. Their substantial and recurring demand for dollars can add to buying pressure in the spot market, potentially weakening the rupee. By meeting their requirements through the special window, the RBI aims to moderate this pressure and facilitate the oil companies’ access to foreign exchange.
The move comes amid rising crude oil prices, which increase India’s import bill and the demand for dollars. As a major importer of crude, India is particularly vulnerable to higher international oil prices, which can widen the trade deficit and weigh on the domestic currency. The RBI has foreign exchange reserves of around $735 billion, providing a substantial buffer to manage external-sector pressures.
The central bank has also recently mobilised more than $127 billion through foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR(B)) deposits and an additional $9 billion through overseas foreign currency borrowings (OFCBs) and external commercial borrowings (ECBs), according to estimates cited in the data.
The special window signals the RBI’s willingness to use its foreign exchange resources to manage short-term market pressures arising from essential imports. However, the extent to which it can contain rupee depreciation will also depend on the trajectory of crude prices, broader dollar movements and overall capital flows.
Experts said factors, including foreign investor, outflows due to lack of artificial intelligence themed stocks in Indian markets, hardening of rates in overseas markets, which offers relatively strong and risk-free returns, and also tightening by other central banks has led to the pressures on the rupee.
On Wednesday, Governor Sanjay Malhotra had assured that the RBI will help stabilise the rupee, which he said was undervalued, and help the currency find its correct value.
The RBI said authorised dealers should not permit users to rebook any foreign exchange derivative contract involving the Rupee (deliverable or non-deliverable), which has been cancelled.
(With inputs from PTI)

briefs.headline: India initiates anti-dumping probe on Pen-G, salts from China
briefs.deck: The DGTR, which agreed to the company’s suggestion for 2025-26 as the period of investigation, said there is sufficient prima facie evidence that the PUC is being dumped into the domestic market by exporters from China.
briefs.bodyText:
India has initiated an anti-dumping investigation into imports of Penicillin G and its salts from China after domestic manufacturer Lyfius Pharma alleged the imports were causing material retardation to the industry.
The company has sought imposition of anti-dumping duties, the Directorate General of Trade Remedies, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said in a notification initiating the investigation.
The Aurobindo Pharma subsidiary began manufacturing Penicillin G more than two years ago under the government’s production linked incentive (PLI) scheme and with it revived production of the beta-lactam antibiotic in the country after about three decades.
Stating that it is the sole eligible producer of the product under consideration (PUC) in India and there are no other domestic manufacturers, Lyfius Pharma, in the application, said India used to previously manufacture Penicillin G before sustained influx of imports ceased domestic production.
The PUC, under the investigation, covers Penicillin G in all forms, grades, strengths and concentrations, along with its salt forms, whether or not conforming to pharmacopoeial standards, and in both solid and liquid forms. The product is used as a key starting material (KSM) and active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) in the manufacture of various medicines used to treat bacterial infections, including pneumonia, dental infections, diphtheria and meningitis, the DGTR said.
The DGTR, which agreed to the company’s suggestion for 2025-26 as the period of investigation, said there is sufficient prima facie evidence that the PUC is being dumped into the domestic market by exporters from China.
Lyfius Pharma said it has not been able to achieve production and sales as expected and forced to reduce its prices to match the landed price of imports.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Lyfius Pharma’s 15,000 tonnes Pen G facility in Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh in October 2024. Aurobindo Pharma had said the facility represented a strategic ₹2,500 crore investment under the Centre’s PLI scheme for pharmaceutical sector.
India manufactured Penicillin G until the late 1980s. However, following globalisation, imports led to closure of all plants producing the antibiotic in the country. In March 2024, then Union Minister for Chemicals and Fertilisers and Health and Family Welfare Mansukh Mandaviya said the government was working on bringing back production of Penicillin G in India after three decades.
Earlier this year, Aurobindo Pharma said it expected to produce more than 10,000 metric tonnes on annualised basis over the following 12 months.
